difficultyReason: Three related factual observations with one clear hedged inference. Distractors are either out-of-scope or overreach into 'all'/'only' territory.
stimulus: A recent survey of primary-care physicians in Valbrook found that those who had taken a one-week course on nutrition counseling were, on average, twice as likely as their colleagues to discuss diet during routine checkups. The survey also found that patients of the course-trained physicians reported making healthier food choices more often than patients of other physicians. No other differences between the two groups of physicians were noted.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Every patient whose physician took the nutrition course now eats a healthier diet than before.

choices.label: B
choices.text: At least some patients make healthier food choices after their physicians discuss diet with them during checkups.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Physicians who take continuing-education courses are generally more competent than those who do not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nutrition counseling is the most effective tool a primary-care physician has for improving patient health.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Patients in Valbrook were less healthy than patients elsewhere before the nutrition course was offered.

explanations.correct: The stimulus links two facts — course-trained physicians discuss diet more often, and their patients report healthier choices more often. The most defensible hedged inference is that at least some patients' improved choices follow from such discussions.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'every patient' is not supported; the stimulus speaks in averages.
explanations.C: Out of scope — the stimulus is about one specific course, not continuing education generally.
explanations.D: Too strong and out of scope — no comparison is made to other tools.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no claim is made about Valbrook patients' prior health.

difficultyReason: Two observational facts about a wetland; correct answer is a modest inference. Traps are overreach and opposite-direction.
stimulus: Biologists studying the Oster Marsh report that populations of the marsh wren have grown substantially in each of the past five years. Over the same period, the marsh's native cattail reeds, in which marsh wrens build their nests, have expanded to cover roughly 30 percent more of the marsh than they did before. No other major changes to the marsh's vegetation or water levels have been recorded.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The marsh wren population would not have grown at all without the expansion of cattail reeds.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any marsh with expanding cattail reeds will see a rise in marsh wren populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The expansion of cattail reeds in Oster Marsh has probably contributed to the growth of its marsh wren population.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Marsh wrens nest only in native cattail reeds and in no other vegetation.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The Oster Marsh contains more marsh wrens than any comparable wetland in the region.

explanations.correct: Cattails are the wrens' nesting habitat, they have expanded substantially, and no other relevant change occurred. The hedged inference that the expansion has probably contributed to the population growth is what the facts most support.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'would not have grown at all' is not supported; the stimulus allows other causes.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus is about one marsh, not any marsh.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus says wrens build nests in cattails, not that they nest nowhere else.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no comparison with other wetlands is made.

difficultyReason: Two commerce facts, one clear hedged conclusion about subgroup behavior. Traps overreach to absolutes.
stimulus: Sales data from Orlen Bookshop show that among customers who purchased a novel during last year's summer discount promotion, more than half also bought at least one full-price book during the same visit. Customers who did not purchase a discounted novel, by contrast, bought a full-price book during their visits less than a quarter of the time.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The summer discount promotion caused Orlen Bookshop's overall revenue to rise.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No customer who bought a full-price book last summer would have done so without the discount promotion.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Customers who purchased a discounted novel tended to spend more at Orlen Bookshop per visit than customers who did not.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Most of Orlen Bookshop's full-price sales last year came from customers buying discounted novels.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The discount promotion will be even more successful if repeated next summer.

explanations.correct: The first group bought a discounted novel plus a full-price book over half the time; the second group bought a full-price book less than a quarter of the time and no discounted novel. The hedged comparative claim about per-visit spending is what the data most strongly support.
explanations.A: Out of scope — the stimulus compares subgroups, not overall revenue.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'no customer ... would have' goes beyond what the data show.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus gives rates per customer group, not the composition of full-price sales overall.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no prediction about future promotions is supported.

difficultyReason: Two legal facts about an appellate court; correct answer applies hedged language to the pattern observed.
stimulus: Of the criminal convictions appealed to the Westhaven Court of Appeals last year, those in which the defense argued that the trial judge had improperly excluded evidence were overturned roughly twice as often as those that raised other grounds for appeal. The court handled a roughly equal number of appeals of each kind.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Trial judges in Westhaven improperly exclude evidence more often than they make other kinds of errors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any appeal arguing that a trial judge improperly excluded evidence will succeed in the Westhaven Court of Appeals.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some of the convictions overturned last year by the Westhaven Court of Appeals were overturned on the ground that a trial judge had improperly excluded evidence.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The Westhaven Court of Appeals applies a less demanding standard to evidentiary-exclusion claims than to other grounds for appeal.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Most convictions that are appealed in Westhaven are ultimately overturned on some ground or other.

explanations.correct: If appeals citing improper exclusion are overturned at roughly twice the rate of other appeals, and the counts are roughly equal, some overturned convictions last year rested on that ground. The hedged 'at least some' claim is directly supported.
explanations.A: Out of scope — frequency of errors is not compared, only success rates on appeal.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'any appeal ... will succeed' is not supported; only a higher success rate is reported.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the stimulus does not describe the court's standards.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no overall overturn rate is given.

difficultyReason: Two archaeological facts yield one hedged historical inference. Traps are scope creep and too-strong.
stimulus: Archaeologists excavating a small coastal settlement dated to roughly 1200 B.C.E. uncovered storage jars containing olive oil whose chemical signature matches oils produced on an island more than 500 kilometers away. The settlement's own soil and climate are unsuitable for olive cultivation, and no evidence of olive presses has been found at the site.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Olive oil was the most widely traded commodity in the region around 1200 B.C.E.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The settlement's inhabitants obtained at least some of their olive oil through long-distance exchange.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The inhabitants of the coastal settlement were wealthier than those of inland settlements of the same period.

choices.label: D
choices.text: No goods other than olive oil were imported into the coastal settlement from distant sources.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The island where the matching oil was produced was the largest olive-oil exporter of its era.

explanations.correct: The oil's chemical signature matches a distant source, and the settlement could not have produced olives or pressed oil locally. The hedged inference that at least some oil reached them through long-distance exchange is what the facts best support.
explanations.A: Too strong and out of scope — the stimulus says nothing about the ranking of traded commodities.
explanations.C: Out of scope — no comparative wealth claim is supported.
explanations.D: Too strong — the stimulus only addresses olive oil.
explanations.E: Too strong — the island's ranking as an exporter is not discussed.

difficultyReason: Straightforward technology observation with one hedged inference; traps include absolute generalization and opposite direction.
stimulus: In a controlled test, engineers measured the fuel consumption of a fleet of delivery trucks before and after installing software that automatically adjusts engine settings based on road grade and speed. Trucks using the software consumed, on average, 8 percent less fuel per kilometer than identical trucks without the software. Driving routes and cargo loads were held constant across both groups.
questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Installing the software reduces fuel consumption by the same amount for every truck that uses it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any technology that adjusts engine settings automatically will lower a truck's fuel consumption.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Trucks equipped with the engine-adjustment software tend to consume less fuel per kilometer than otherwise comparable trucks without it.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The software reduces fuel consumption primarily by lowering engine speed on steep grades.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fleet operators who adopt the software will recoup its purchase cost within a year.

explanations.correct: Identical trucks on identical routes with identical loads differed only in whether they used the software, and the software-equipped trucks averaged 8 percent lower fuel use. The hedged comparative generalization tracks exactly what was measured.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'same amount for every truck' goes beyond an 8 percent average.
explanations.B: Too strong — the stimulus is about one specific software package.
explanations.D: Out of scope — the mechanism behind the savings is not discussed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — no claim about purchase cost or payback period is supported.

difficultyReason: Two linguistics observations yield one hedged inference about an exception to a broader pattern.
stimulus: In most of the world's languages, words denoting close kin such as 'mother' and 'father' tend to be short and to use only the simplest consonants. In the Ikwe language, however, the word for 'mother' is four syllables long and contains several consonants that young children acquire only after age five. Ikwe-speaking children, linguists report, typically begin using the word for 'mother' noticeably later than children acquiring other languages do.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Ikwe-speaking children are generally slower than other children to acquire language overall.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A word's phonetic complexity can affect how early children acquire it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every language in which kinship terms are long and phonetically complex delays children's acquisition of those terms.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Ikwe speakers use a different word when addressing their mothers in everyday speech.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Short words with simple consonants are easier for adults to learn than long words with complex consonants.

explanations.correct: The stimulus presents a cross-linguistic pattern and one case where a kinship word is unusually long and complex; children in that case acquire the word later. The hedged inference that phonetic complexity can affect acquisition timing is the one most supported.
explanations.A: Out of scope — only one word's acquisition is discussed, not overall language acquisition.
explanations.C: Too strong — a single case does not support a universal claim.
explanations.D: Out of scope — everyday usage patterns are not discussed.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus concerns children, not adult learners.

difficultyReason: Two arts facts suggest one modest inference about attendance and programming. Traps overreach or are opposite-direction.
stimulus: The Mercer Civic Theater reports that performances featuring works by living local playwrights sold, on average, about 20 percent more tickets last season than performances of works by better-known historical playwrights. Ticket prices, performance dates, and marketing budgets were comparable for both kinds of program.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the statements above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Works by living local playwrights are of higher artistic quality than works by historical playwrights.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Mercer Civic Theater audiences last season tended to prefer works by living local playwrights over works by better-known historical playwrights.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Mercer Civic Theater will stop staging works by historical playwrights in future seasons.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Every performance by a living local playwright at Mercer Civic Theater sold out last season.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Audiences at other theaters in the region showed similar preferences last season.

explanations.correct: With ticket prices, dates, and marketing held comparable, the difference in average ticket sales most directly supports a hedged preference claim about Mercer's audiences last season.
explanations.A: Out of scope and too strong — artistic quality is not discussed.
explanations.C: Out of scope — no programming decision is supported.
explanations.D: Too strong — averages do not support a sold-out claim about every performance.
explanations.E: Out of scope — other theaters are not discussed.

difficultyReason: Two policy facts with a clean hedged inference about cause. Traps include absolute claims and opposite-direction alternatives.
stimulus: After the town of Halbrook began offering free evening bus service along three main routes last year, average evening car traffic on those routes decreased by about 15 percent over the following six months. On comparable routes in Halbrook that received no free evening bus service, evening car traffic during the same period was essentially unchanged.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Free evening bus service was the only factor that could have reduced evening car traffic on the three routes.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Residents of Halbrook generally prefer bus travel to car travel.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Every Halbrook resident who took a free evening bus along one of the three routes would otherwise have driven a car.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The introduction of free evening bus service in Halbrook likely contributed to the drop in evening car traffic on the three routes.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Halbrook's free evening bus service will produce similar reductions if extended to every route in town.

explanations.correct: Traffic fell on exactly the routes that received free buses and held steady on comparable routes that did not. The hedged causal inference is what the pattern most strongly supports.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'only factor' is not supported; the comparison makes the free service a likely contributor, not the sole one.
explanations.B: Too strong — a general preference is broader than what the traffic pattern shows.
explanations.C: Too strong — 'every ... would otherwise have driven' goes well beyond the data.
explanations.E: Out of scope — extending the program town-wide is not addressed.

difficultyReason: Two ethics-survey facts yield one natural hedged inference. Traps are too-strong universals and out-of-scope predictions.
stimulus: In a recent anonymous survey of accountants at large firms, more than 70 percent reported that they had at some point been asked by a supervisor to record a transaction in a way they believed misleading. Of those respondents, a clear majority said they had complied with the request at least once because they feared professional retaliation.
questionStem: The statements above most strongly support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Most accountants at large firms routinely misrepresent the financial position of the companies they audit.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Any accountant who complies with a supervisor's misleading request does so only out of fear of retaliation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: At least some accountants at large firms have recorded transactions in ways they considered misleading out of fear of professional retaliation.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Supervisors at large accounting firms are generally indifferent to the ethical concerns of their staff.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Stronger whistleblower protections would eliminate misleading accounting at large firms.

explanations.correct: A majority of the more-than-70-percent group said they had complied at least once out of fear of retaliation. The hedged 'at least some' inference about those accountants' conduct is a direct and modest reading of the numbers.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'routinely misrepresent' goes beyond having complied at least once in some cases.
explanations.B: Too strong — 'only out of fear of retaliation' is not supported; other motives are not ruled out.
explanations.D: Out of scope — supervisors' general attitudes are not described.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope — the effect of whistleblower protections is not addressed.
